articles.title: I’ve had a stinking cold this week – and I’m longing for good advice | Adrian Chiles
articles.summary: Heavy and light colds tend to pass more quickly than middle-of-the-road ones. But should I stay in bed or continue mixing with others? How to define the cold that’s ruining your day? There’s a hierarchy. We start with the sniffle, the mere runny nose, scratchy throat or just feeling a little off.
body: The only good thing about the stinking cold is that you have the green light to do sod all and repair to bed. This was me for three days this week, and it has firmed up a theory I have long held that you’re better off getting a stinker because it tends to come and go and be done with more quickly than the other varieties. This theory, I should point out, is based on my lived experience rather than any clinical expertise or any kind of research. Sorry – I felt too ill to bother with anything of the kind.

The kind of cold I really can’t bear is the middle-of-the-road, magnolia, vanilla, neither-here-nor-there type. When you don’t feel up to doing much, but neither, if you’re honest, are you feeling ropey enough to justify doing nothing. And these kinds of colds, for me anyway, seem to drag on for ever.

But seriously, what do you do? What’s the right call for your own health and for others in your workplace or friendship group? Do you stay at home for the greater good, or do you soldier on bravely and be quietly commended for toughing it out, while running the risk of infecting friends, enemies and workmates with a dose of whatever you’ve got?
points: Heavy and light colds tend to pass more quickly than middle-of-the-road ones.

articles.title: ‘A web of canals and cobbled streets’: a city break in Haarlem in the Netherlands
articles.summary: A short ride from Amsterdam, this laid-back city has great museums, cosy bars and a new exhibition featuring the works of Rembrandt and local artist Frans Hals this winter.
body: I t’s only 15 minutes away from the Dutch capital by train, but Haarlem feels a million miles from Amsterdam, and perhaps provides a more typical glimpse of the Netherlands than trailing around the well-worn tourist trail of Van Gogh, coffee shops and red lights. An attractive city of cobbled streets, gabled houses and canals, Haarlem is, as the Dutch would say, a gezellig sort of place – cosy, convivial, and full of intriguing nooks and corners. I’ve been coming here for years, and it seems odd that Haarlem is not better known, at least to UK visitors.

This winter there’s the added draw of an exhibition devoted to the works of a local boy, the 17th-century painter Frans Hals, and his better-known contemporary Rembrandt in the city’s Frans Hals Museum (until 28 February 2027). No one really knows whether these two titans of the Dutch Golden Age of the 16th and 17th centuries ever met, but seeing their work hung together like this is powerful and compelling. The museum used to be the Oudemannenhuis (Old Men’s House), a retirement and care home where Hals lived out his final penniless years.
points: A short ride from Amsterdam, this laid-back city has great museums, cosy bars and a new exhibition featuring the works of Rembrandt and local artist Frans Hals this winter.

articles.title: Rachel Roddy’s recipe for torta tenerina, or rich chocolate cake | A kitchen in Rome
articles.summary: This soft-but-dense, velvety delight is cake at its most pudding-like. It’s at its prime still warm from the oven, but gets gloriously fudgy after a night in the fridge. The note by Elizabeth David is helpful here: “This cake can also be eaten like a pudding” for its soft-dense-velvet-texture.
body: Having just mentioned fact-checking, I am now going to side-step the origin stories. The name, however, more or less translates as “little tender one”, although that “little” refers more to the fact that it is a bit tender, rather than being on the small side. Especially because tenerina recipes from Ferrara call for tins ranging from 24-26cm in size, which produce slender cakes that are gently cracked on top and tacolenta (sticky) within; in fact, another name for the cake is torta tacolenta.

A timer is to forgetful cooks what a microwave is to melting chocolate: that is, invaluable. Otherwise, use a bain-marie or bowl balanced over (but not touching) simmering water in a pan. It is an important step to separate the eggs, so they can be added in two stages. First the yolks beaten with the sugar; then the whites beaten to stiff peaks and folded in gently to protect the air that’s been so carefully incorporated. Regarding the flour, it can be substituted for ground almonds, hazelnuts or pine nuts, all of which produce an almost identical texture, alongside lovely flavour; they also turn the cake into what could be called a torta caprese.

articles.title: ‘Christmas is all in the preparation!’ Chefs on eight easy things to do now – so you can relax on the big day
articles.summary: No one wants to slog away in the kitchen while everyone else gets festive. Thanks to these hacks and recipes from professionals, you won’t have to. When it comes to cooking during the festive season, time is tight, fridge space is at a premium and the last thing you want is to be trapped in the…
body: From freezable, deeply delicious gravy to flavoured butters guaranteed to give the driest of meats a juicy kick, from preserves to liven up leftovers to lightweight puddings the whole family can enjoy, I tested the recipes chefs recommend making now to guarantee your Christmas larder is well stocked, no matter who ends up at your dining table.

Rather than reaching for granules or spending your time scraping remnants from the bottom of a roasting tray while juggling other dishes, prepare a concentrated gravy ahead of time and keep it in the freezer or the fridge until you need it. Martyn Wilson, the head chef at Timberyard in Edinburgh, recommends roasting about 1kg of chicken wings and turkey drumsticks in a 200C oven for 40 minutes, until they take on a dark brown caramelisation, then adding them to a large pot with chopped onion, carrots, celery, a teaspoon of peppercorns and a tied bundle of thyme, rosemary and bay leaves. Cover with water and simmer for two to three hours before straining.

articles.title: Ariana Grande Brings Her Two Great Loves—Ricky Álvarez and Rare Vintage—to the Red Carpet
articles.summary: Making their red carpet debut at the “Focker-in-Law” premiere in New York, Grande and her rekindled beau Ricky couldn’t keep their hands off each other.
body: Ariana Grande brought two of her greatest loves to the red carpet last night: boyfriend Ricky Álvarez and a very, very good piece of vintage.

At the New York premiere of Focker-in-Law, the singer and actor made her first red carpet appearance with Álvarez since rekindling their romance earlier this year. And if their constant embraces, adoring glances, and kisses were anything to go by, the pair are very much still in the honeymoon phase.

Stylist Law Roach selected a vintage 1990s Badgley Mischka gown for the occasion. The delicate, spaghetti-strapped design featured a pale silver-gray windowpane check, a fitted bodice scattered with tiny beaded flowers, and a voluminous floor-skimming skirt. She accessorized with Swarovski Matrix hoop earrings—a recent favorite—and traded the flipped bob she’s been sporting of late for a sleek micro ponytail, tied with a little ivory ribbon. Makeup was also her go-to style of glowy and highlight-dominant.
points: Making their red carpet debut at the “Focker-in-Law” premiere in New York, Grande and her rekindled beau Ricky couldn’t keep their hands off each other.

articles.title: Andy Baraghani's Ditto Cafe Is His Most Personal Project Yet
articles.summary: The former BA editor spent years tailoring his cooking for everyone else. A Ditto, his NYC counter-service café, he’s finally serving food entirely on his own terms.
body: Andy Baraghani is more afraid of becoming stagnant than he is of dying. Stagnancy, he’s quick to clarify, is different from stillness. Stagnancy is like a fetid pond; stillness is meditative. Baraghani seems to be at risk of neither.

It is late morning on the first actually chilly day of autumn and we are staring one another down across a stainless-steel prep table, which has been dragooned into use as an island in his outrageously good-looking kitchen. He is about to make me scones—salty-sweet ones with dates and lemon zest, an offering under development for his forthcoming café Ditto. But first, we’ll need to pop out for cream.
Quite literally in motion since I arrived, Baraghani finishes his point on stagnancy: He fears a life in which he is not learning, moving, or evolving “as a writer, a cook, and a good gay,” he says.

A Ditto, his NYC counter-service café, he’s finally serving food entirely on his own terms.

articles.title: On the Podcast: Léa Seydoux Has a Shopping Problem. Plus: WNBA Star Gabby Williams!
articles.summary: For this Thursday’s episode of “The Run-Through,” Léa Seydoux sat down with Chloe Malle and Taylor Antrim to discuss her two latest films, both of which she shot shortly after giving birth to her second child.
body: More than a decade after winning the Palme d’Or for her role in 2013’s B lue Is the Warmest Color, Léa Seydoux—the self-proclaimed “queen of Cannes” —has confidently made the seaside city and festival her domain. Just earlier this year, she was there to celebrate two of her latest projects: Marie Kreutzer’s Gentle Monster, which comes to Netflix on November 18, and Arthur Harari’s The Unknown.

“I used this body as a tool,” she explained. “Most of the time you see actresses with bodies that are very controlled, especially here in America. And if I can speak for myself, I’m a bit tired of seeing all these bodies that are just very skinny and not very real. I’m proud to show this body that we’re not used to seeing onscreen.”

The group also got into Seydoux’s long-time friendship with fellow French actress Adèle Exarchopoulos, who sported a “Léa Forever” T-shirt at Cannes this year. “We have a great relationship,” Seydoux said of her Blue Is the Warmest Color co-star. “I mean, we grew up together. She’s a great inspiration as well. I love her freedom—the way she’s not polished, you know? She is herself and very genuine.”

articles.title: The Great Bear Rainforest: How Fashion Rallied to Stop the Deforestation of an Ancient Rainforest
articles.summary: The Great Bear Rainforest is one of the world’s most critical carbon sinks, and fashion was unknowingly contributing to its demise.
body: This story is part of ‘The Business Case for Nature’, a series exploring fashion’s impact on nature and vice versa.

The Great Bear Rainforest, spanning 6.4 million hectares from the Alaskan border to just above Vancouver Island, is the largest coastal temperate rainforest in the world, a critical carbon sink, and the only known home of the extremely rare white-furred spirit bear. Whales migrate through the rainforest year-round, and it is a major breeding ground for all five species of Pacific salmon. Thanks to the region’s heavy rainfall and nutrient-rich ecosystem, it also houses an array of ancient trees over a thousand years old, including sitka spruce (among the tallest trees in the world) and red western cedar (which hold deep cultural significance for the 26 local First Nations).
points: The Great Bear Rainforest is one of the world’s most critical carbon sinks, and fashion was unknowingly contributing to its demise.

articles.title: Grace Cacciato Wins the 2026–2027 S.Pellegrino Young Chef Academy U.S. Regional Final
articles.summary: Ten chefs. Five hours in the Bon Appétit Test Kitchen. One ticket to Milan. Meet the competitors of the 2026–2027 S.Pellegrino Young Chef Academy U.S. Regional Final.
body: The 10 chefs vying to win the region cooked in the Bon Appétit Test Kitchen in New York City on Monday, and the winner was announced the following evening at the U.S. Regional Final Gala & Awards. Everyone enjoyed the Gala menu, crafted by chef Garrett Brower, the 2024-25 U.S. winner who is the chef de cuisine at Bresca in Washington, D.C. and global mentor chef Aisha Ibrahim.

Representing the Michelin-starred restaurant Saga in New York, Cacciato presented a dish that featured the most components of any in the competition. All the judges were impressed with her sauce work and bold flavors.

Saga executive chef Charlie Mitchell returned for his second year as a mentor, working alongside Cacciato, a repeat competitor. “It was nice to see how her brain works…getting her perspective was inspiring,” he said. Cacciato was equally enthusiastic. “It’s the best competition, and everyone wants to be a part of it,” she said.
